seats: a secular academic scholar of the Bible

fixes.row: What stands between wrath and the people: an intercessor, a priest, a zealous man, the blood, the atoning sacrifice
fixes.why: The label itself says the atoning sacrifice stands between wrath and the people. That is the propitiation reading, stated as the row's heading, while the note admits none of the four verses has a wrath word (the Berean prints none, and I read Rom 3:25 and 1 John 4:10 as sacrifice-for-sin, nothing more). A label must say only what its verses say; a note under a tilted label does not undo it. The row also welds the OT picture (Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, Jeremiah turn wrath aside in the same scene) to four NT verses that carry no wrath word, so the OT figures read as types of the NT sacrifice.
fixes.fix: Relabel to what the verses with wrath words say: 'Wrath turned aside: Moses stands in the breach, Aaron's censer, Phinehas' zeal, Jeremiah's and Daniel's prayer; “saved from wrath through Him”' (Exod 32:12, Num 16:46, Num 25:11, Ps 106:23, Jer 18:20, Dan 9:16, Rom 5:9). Move Rom 3:25, Heb 2:17, 1 John 2:2, 4:10 into a separate short row 'The atoning sacrifice (the Berean's words)' with the existing note kept as written, door atonement. Keep OT verses leading.

fixes.row: What stands between wrath and the people
fixes.why: Ps 78:38 has God Himself forgiving and restraining His anger, with no intercessor, priest or zealous man standing between. It fits the label only through the note's later reading.
fixes.fix: Drop from this row (it already stands in 'Anger and mercy' and 'Anger turned away').

fixes.row: Wrath and judgment, vengeance; the ruler who brings wrath on the wrongdoer
fixes.why: Rule 6 and the Berean. The note quotes Rom 13:4 as 'an avenger who brings wrath on the wrongdoer', but the Berean prints 'an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer' (13:4) and 'to avoid punishment' (13:5); no English wrath word appears in either, so the example shown to the reader does not show the label. The wrath word is the Greek ὀργή only. The label also carries a 2-verse detail out of 21.
fixes.fix: Reword the note to the Berean's words and say the Greek: 'Rom 13:4 reads “an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” and 13:5 “to avoid punishment”; the Greek word in both is ὀργή, wrath.' Shorten the label to 'Wrath and judgment, vengeance'; the note carries the ruler. Keep Rom 13:4-5 out of the first four examples.

fixes.row: The day of wrath; wrath to come, and shelter from it
fixes.why: The label and its note speak of 'wrath to come' and 'when the coming wrath comes'. Twelve of the OT verses are a day of anger that has already fallen (Lam 2:1 'in the day of His anger' is Jerusalem's fall, past; Zephaniah is the coming of Babylon) or a proverbial day (Prov 11:4). Filing them under 'wrath to come' reads the New Testament's future-eschatological frame (Matt 3:7, 1 Thess 1:10) back onto prophets who describe a historical day. 1 Thess 2:16 says wrath 'has come upon them', not 'to come', and sits under the same label. The three OT-first examples are also not OT-first: three of the four shown are NT.
fixes.fix: Split in two. (1) 'The day of the LORD's anger' for the OT verses (Zeph 1:15, 1:18, 2:2-3, Lam 1:12, 2:1, 2:21-22, Isa 13:13, Job 20:28, 21:30, Ps 110:5, Prov 11:4, Ezek 7:19, Isa 26:20, Job 14:13), no 'to come' wording, OT examples first. (2) 'The coming wrath, and being saved from it' for Matt 3:7, Luke 3:7, Rom 2:5, 5:9, 1 Thess 1:10, 5:9, Rev 6:16-17, with the existing note. Move 1 Thess 2:16 and Luke 21:23 out of both to a row or note that says wrath 'has come' ('the utmost wrath has come upon them'; 'wrath against this people'). Because the verb tense differs, leave the page not saying when.

fixes.row: The anger of the LORD, the wrath of God
fixes.why: Of 68 verses about 55 are the Hebrew Scriptures, yet the first examples a reader sees are Rom 1:18, then Exod 4:14, John 3:36, Rev 19:15: three of four are NT, with the Romans verse leading, so the heading reads as Paul's phrase. The story's own arc (the anger that burns in Numbers and Judges, the formula in Exod 34) is not what the reader meets first.
fixes.fix: Reorder `lead` so the OT comes first: Exod 4:14, Num 11:1/Num 25:3, Deut 6:15 or Josh 7:1, then Rom 1:18. Keep the note as written.

fixes.row: Anger against Israel, Judah and Jerusalem
fixes.why: Luke 21:23 ('wrath against this people') is the second example shown, before any OT verse, though the row is almost wholly OT. It also appears with 1 Thess 2:16 elsewhere, while 1 Thess 2:16 is not here, so the NT treatment of the same kind of verse is inconsistent. 2 Kgs 3:27 ('great wrath against Israel', whose wrath the verse does not say) sits among God's anger with no flag.
fixes.fix: Put Luke 21:23 last in the row's verse list (not among the first four examples); treat it and 1 Thess 2:16 alike (see the day-of-wrath fix). Add to the row note: 'In 2 Kgs 3:27 the verse does not say whose wrath it is.'

fixes.row: Slow to anger; patience beside wrath  /  Anger and mercy, compassion, favor, forgiveness
fixes.why: Eight of the 17 verses in the mercy row are the same Exodus 34:6 formula that already fills the 'slow to anger' row (15). The formula is the story's own centre, answered again and again in Numbers, Nehemiah, Psalms, Joel, Jonah; it has been cut into two rows whose examples repeat (Exod 34:6 and Ps 103:8 lead both). The 'slow to anger' row also mixes the formula said of the LORD with the proverbs on a person who is slow to anger (Prov 14:29, 16:32, Jas 1:19) as if one thing.
fixes.fix: Merge the two into 'Slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion: the formula after Exod 34:6, and the anger beside mercy' (Exod 34:6, Num 14:18, Neh 9:17, Ps 86:15, 103:8, 145:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, Nah 1:3, Ps 30:5, Isa 54:8, Mic 7:18, Hos 11:9, Rom 9:22). Move the human sayings (Prov 14:29, 15:18, 16:32, Jas 1:19) to the person's-anger row. Keep the note. That brings the count down by one.

fixes.why: These are sayings about a hot-tempered person, shown among God's anger at sin and idols. The builder's own rule is that human anger is kept apart from God's.

fixes.row: Anger against the nations, enemies and the wicked
fixes.why: Isa 14:6 is the tyrant king of Babylon's rage that struck the peoples, not God's anger against them. Prov 11:23 says the wicked's hope brings wrath, with no nations or enemies in view. Both sit beside God's anger on the nations and read as the same thing.
fixes.fix: Move Isa 14:6 to 'Anger in the stories, and a king's wrath' (or a person's anger); drop Prov 11:23 into the sin/wicked row or 'Every other use'.

fixes.row: Anger that burns, is kindled, flares like fire  /  Anger turned away, or not turned away
fixes.why: Two of the largest rows (74 and 48) hold the LORD's anger and a person's together, though the hub says human anger gets its own rows. The fourth example in the fire row is Jacob angry with Rachel, directly after three of God's. The reader cannot tell the two apart from the label.
fixes.fix: Add a note to both rows: 'These rows hold both the LORD's anger and people's; each verse shows whose.' Optionally put people's anger first-flagged by verb-form.

fixes.row: An oath sworn in anger: “they shall never enter My rest”
fixes.why: The quoted words are Ps 95:11 and Heb 3:11; Deut 1:34 and Num 32:10 swear that the generation will not see the land and do not say 'rest'. The label puts a later text's phrase on the earlier ones, and the first examples shown do not show it.
fixes.fix: Relabel: 'An oath sworn in anger: that generation shall not enter the land; “they shall never enter My rest”'. Keep Deut 1:34 and Ps 95:11 first, Hebrews after, as now.

fixes.row: What Jesus and the letters say of a person's anger
fixes.why: Rule 6: the quoted words are not the Berean's. The Berean reads 'anyone who is angry with his brother' (not 'everyone'), 'man's anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires', and 'Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger'. The label quotes another translation. Also Eph 4:26 quotes Ps 4:4, so an OT root exists with no sign of it.
fixes.fix: Replace the label quotes with the Berean's: “anyone who is angry with his brother”, “Be angry, yet do not sin”, “man's anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires”, “Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger”. Add to the row note that Eph 4:26 quotes Psalm 4:4.

fixes.row: Children of wrath, vessels of wrath
fixes.why: The note treats only Eph 2:3 'by nature'. Rom 9:22 ('vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction') is the other half of the row title and the verse where traditions part on who prepared them; the row puts it beside Eph 2:3 as if the two were one group, and the page says nothing there. Also the two options offered for 'by nature' (inherited sin, or the course each follows) leave out the plain 'by birth / in our former condition' of Eph 2:1-3, so the note names two doctrinal answers and omits the text's own plain frame ('you ... all of us once lived').
fixes.fix: Extend the note: 'In Rom 9:22 readers part on who prepared the vessels, God or those who are in them; the page takes no side.' Reword the 'by nature' sentence to begin with what the verse says ('Paul says this of “all of us” who once followed the cravings of the flesh') before 'readers part'. Do not state the two options as the only two.

fixes.row: Cries to the LORD about His anger
fixes.why: Hab 3:2 is the last example shown and its word chip is empty: the Hebrew is רֹגֶז, which is not in the hub's words (the spec names it only in the report). The reader sees no original word, and the verse is the key one for the arc (anger and mercy remembered).
fixes.fix: Add h7264 רֹגֶז to the 'others' with the verse Hab 3:2, or give the example a word chip in the row.

fixes.why: A row of 2 verses that is mostly a note. Rule 7 asks for fewer rows; the hub is 26 against a 15-25 target.
fixes.fix: Drop the row; put its note on the verb form as a form-level note, and leave Ps 2:12 and Deut 9:22 out of both rows.

worker_points.point: What turns wrath away (row 17: four verses with no wrath word)
worker_points.why: Including them is acceptable only if the label does not assert that the sacrifice stands between wrath and the people; as written it does. Separate the four ἱλ- verses and relabel as above. The sacrifice hub's 'Lord's table' parallel does not carry over, because that row had its own words in the verses.
The note is nearer to neutral than most, but names two doctrinal answers as if they were the only two, and does not touch Rom 9:22. See fix.

worker_points.point: What the wrath of God is (row 1 note)
worker_points.why: It cites Rom 1:24, 26, 28 ('gave them over'), which the verses say, and takes no side. The row order is the real tilt (see lead order fix), not the note.

worker_points.point: Wrath to come (row 4) and the oath (row 13)
worker_points.why: The 'wrath to come' label is wrong for twelve OT verses that describe a day already fallen; the oath label quotes Ps 95 over Deut 1:34. See fixes.

Rev 6:16-17 and Mark 3:5 name the Lamb and Jesus; 1 Thess 1:10 shows Jesus as deliverer from the wrath, not its agent, and the label says so in its own quotation. Keeping Rev 19:15 under God is right; the verse does not name Jesus. Four verses is thin but honest.

Hard verses kept, labelled in the text's own words, nothing softened. A secular reader would want them kept visible exactly like this. A short sentence that they are prayers in the speaker's voice is not needed; the label already says 'Asked of God'.

worker_points.point: Human anger rows 20-22, 25, and Eph 4:26 as command or concession
worker_points.why: Leaving Eph 4:26 without a note is right; the verse is shown. Only add that it quotes Ps 4:4. The move of Prov 19:11, 22:24, 29:22 and the mixed fire/turned-away rows (see fixes) is needed for the separation to hold.
The note misquotes the Berean; the Berean's English has no wrath at all in either verse. See fix.
Leaving whom 'He' means in Ps 2:12 unchosen is correct. Naming the θυμός 'passion' in the catch-all note is the original arbitrating; keep it.

worker_points.point: Translation findings (1 Sam 15:11; Deut 9:22; Job 19:29; Prov 25:15; Rev 14:8)
worker_points.why: Leaving them out of rows where the English shows no label is right. Recording them as findings is the original arbitrating.

worker_points.point: Builder gaps (God vs person by rule; verb frames; add only for seen verses)
worker_points.why: Hand picks suit rule 3; the cost is a 67-verse catch-all that the note describes honestly. The catch-all is large enough to hide God's anger of the prophets that a reader looks for: consider the rows above first.

missing.what: Wrath as the covenant's own curse: Josiah finds the book of the law and the LORD's wrath poured out because the fathers did not keep it; Deut 29's 'his anger and jealousy will burn against that man, and every curse written in this book'; Lev 26. The law row has only 6 verses and the lead names Deut 29:20 and 2 Chr 34:21, but neither is in it (I read both: Deut 29:20 shows 'covenant' in the original and 'every curse written in this book'; 2 Chr 34:21 shows wrath poured out because they did not keep the word). This is the OT's central frame for wrath and it is thinner than Rom 4:15.

Psalm 4:4, the verse Eph 4:26 quotes, so the NT 'be angry' is heard on its OT terms first. The word is רגז (not in the hub); add as a one-verse example under the person's-anger row or the others list.

Jonah 4's own thread: Jonah's anger (4:1, 4:4, 4:9) is in the person's-anger row, and God's formula (4:2) in two others, but nothing lets a reader hear them as one story answering Exodus 34:6; Exod 34 -> Jonah 4 is the clearest arc of the concept. A note on the merged formula row naming Jonah 4:1-4 as the formula said back to God would do.

examples_checked: 12 of 26 rows' examples read in the Berean and shown by their label (all but those flagged: Rom 13:4 and Hab 3:2 show no wrath word; the Ps 2:12/Deut 9:22 catch-all row has no examples to check); the rest checked by the printed text only
summary: The hub is true to the text in most rows and the divine persons are by hand, but the propitiation row's label itself states one reading, the 'wrath to come' row files twelve OT verses under a future-eschatological heading, and the Rom 13 note quotes words the Berean does not print. Fix those, merge the two rows that hold the same Exodus 34:6 formula, and move the human-anger intruders out of God's rows, and it can ship.
